text_lines.fact: The accounts are prepared on the assumption the company continues as a going concern, and the notes explain the doubts at length: losses and negative operating cash in every period since it started.
text_lines.src: eqix-10q-2002q1 p.6 note 1; eqix-10q-2002q2 p.6-8 note 1

text_lines.fact: Quarter 2: the company breached its bank covenants, including a revenue target. The banks agreed a waiver on condition that at least $100m of bonds are converted into shares by a fixed date; otherwise the company is in breach again. The company says it may need to seek bankruptcy protection to force the conversion.
The largest facility was finished in Quarter 1. Nothing is under construction, and there are no plans to build or expand unless new funding is found.
text_lines.src: eqix-10q-2002q1 p.9 note 5; eqix-10q-2002q2 p.10 note 5

text_lines.fact: Large customers have been cutting the capacity they are committed to pay for, often in exchange for longer terms. The company says it has renegotiated all seven of its largest customers and expects no further significant cuts.

Part of revenue is equipment bought from and resold through two companies whose executives sit on this company's board; it is booked at the full sale price. The company says it does not expect significant resales in future.
The main equipment inside the facilities is depreciated over seven to ten years, and building works over no longer than the lease, with leases running up to twenty-three years out.
text_lines.src: 2001 10-K405 critical accounting policies; eqix-10q-2002q2 lease table

text_lines.fact: Several customers, including large carriers, have filed for bankruptcy; aged balances from two of them were written off or fully reserved in Quarter 2.

management_statements_source.gist: Expects the company's own operating-profit measure to move toward breakeven over the next few quarters, through growth in core revenue and tight control of spending.
Intends to issue a significant number of new shares to retire its remaining bonds, and says bondholders have indicated willingness.
Warns that if demand for the kind of service it sells does not keep growing, a viable market for its facilities may not emerge.
Competes with larger, better-funded providers of similar space that could cut prices, and with others copying its model.

strip_hazards: Customer names (the largest customer, and bankrupt customers including the Case A company and other carriers) — remove entirely
Contractor name, landlord names, city and country names, acreage of the ground lease — remove
Share counts, option exercise prices, per-share losses, share price in warrant valuations — omit (reveal price collapse and scale)
Bond coupon (13%) and floating-rate figures — omit (date the period)
Stock-exchange listing risk — keep only as 'the company's shares risk losing their listing', no exchange name, no price threshold
Year references in maturity tables — convert to 'within 1 year', '2-3 years', 'after 5 years'
Terrorism and regional power-shortage risk factors — omit (date the period)
design_notes: Case B looks worse than Case A on almost every line (going concern, covenant breach, bonds priced near a third of face). That is the intended trap: students who called Case A a bubble on debt and losses will call this one the same way.

The lines that point the other way are small and quiet: construction has stopped, operating cash burn is modest, customer count still rising, cost cuts real, and bonds being swapped for equity instead of defaulting.
